source_text:
Epistula (e cod. Barocc. gr. 131)
Εὖ γέ σοι τῆς θαυμασίας ἐπιστολῆς· ὡς ἔαρος ἡμῖν προσέβαλε λογικοῦ, καὶ μουσικόν
τι λίαν ἀντὶ τῶν χελιδόνων ἠχεῖ. ὡς ἔνθους εἰμί τις ὑφ' ἡδονῆς, πάντα θαυμάζων,
τὴν λέξιν, τὸν νοῦν, τὴν ἁρμονίαν, τὸν γράψαντα. καί μοι δοκῶ Λυδὸς ἐξαίφνης
εἶναι, τὰ Λυδῶν μιμησάμενος, οἳ τῷ ∆ιονύσῳ προσκείμενοι μόνον ἔαρ ἦγον ἡνίκα δὴ
καὶ τύχοι παρ' αὐτοῖς ὁ ∆ιόνυσος. ἀλλὰ μὲν ἴσως ταῦτα γελάσεις, ὡς αὐτόχρημα τὸ
σοφιστικὸν ἐπανθεῖ αὐτοῖς, καί με τυχὸν ὡς ἐν ὀνείδει καλέσειας σοφιστήν· ἐγὼ δὲ
τὰ καλὰ μὴ θαυμάζειν οὐκ ἔχω, κἂν σιωπήσῃς, ὦ λῷστε, τἀναντία φθεγγόμεθα·
ἀλλὰ μή μοι διδόναι πρᾶγμα ζητοῦντι τὴν ἐκ τῆς σιωπῆς λύπην παραστῆσαι τοῖς
γράμμασιν.
thought_title: Praise of a letter as rational spring and music
orientation: Procopius opens his letter by thanking the recipient for a letter that has delighted him, and he will go on to defend his enthusiastic praise and ask the recipient not to stay silent.
pass_a_gloss: Well indeed for you for the wonderful letter; as it brought to us a rational spring, and it sounds something very musical instead of the swallows. As I am someone inspired by pleasure, admiring everything, the wording, the thought, the harmony, the writer. And I suddenly think I have become a Lydian, having imitated the Lydians, who, devoted to Dionysus, observed spring only whenever Dionysus also happened to be among them. But perhaps you will laugh at these things, as sheer sophistry blooms upon them, and perhaps you would call me, as in reproach, a sophist; but I am not able not to admire beautiful things, even if you fall silent, best of men, I speak against it; but do not give me trouble, as I seek to represent in writing the grief that comes from silence.

choices.term: Εὖ γέ σοι τῆς θαυμασίας ἐπιστολῆς
choices.english: Well indeed for you for the wonderful letter
choices.why: Keeps the exclamatory genitive of cause and the second-person dative of advantage, preserving the congratulatory force without smoothing it into a full sentence.
rejected: You have done well with your wonderful letter

choices.why: Uses the glossary English for this fixed term, keeping the adjective literal rather than substituting a more idiomatic phrase.

choices.term: μουσικόν τι λίαν ἀντὶ τῶν χελιδόνων ἠχεῖ
choices.english: it sounds something very musical instead of the swallows
choices.why: Preserves the indefinite τι with the adjective, the adverb λίαν, and the substitution expressed by ἀντί with the genitive, without normalizing the syntax.
rejected: it rings out with music in place of swallows
it sounds a very musical note instead of the swallows

choices.term: ὡς ἔνθους εἰμί τις ὑφ' ἡδονῆς
choices.english: As I am someone inspired by pleasure
choices.why: Keeps the ὡς clause, the indefinite τις, and the passive sense of being under the influence of pleasure, matching the source's word order and force.
rejected: I am as if possessed by pleasure
I am quite transported with pleasure

choices.term: τὰ καλὰ μὴ θαυμάζειν οὐκ ἔχω
choices.english: I am not able not to admire beautiful things
choices.why: Renders the double negation literally to preserve the emphatic assertion of inability, rather than converting it to a positive statement.
rejected: I cannot help admiring what is beautiful
I am unable to refrain from admiring beautiful things

choices.why: Keeps the first-person plural verb and the neuter plural object literally, preserving the abruptness of the aside without supplying an implied object.

pass_b_english: You have done well indeed with your wonderful letter. It has brought us a rational spring, and in place of swallows it sounds something very musical. I am as one transported by pleasure, admiring everything: the wording, the thought, the harmony, the writer. And I suddenly think I am a Lydian, imitating the Lydians, who, devoted to Dionysus, observed spring only when Dionysus happened to be present among them. But perhaps you will laugh at this, since sophistry plainly blooms in it, and perhaps you will call me a sophist as a reproach. Yet I am not able not to admire beautiful things; even if you keep silence, my good friend, we speak the opposite. But do not, while I seek, give me the task of representing in writing the grief that comes from silence.

problems.quote: when I seek to avoid it
problems.why: 'ζητοῦντι' is dative participle modifying 'me' (the one seeking), not 'when I seek to avoid it.' The grief is what Procopius seeks; he asks not to be given the task of representing grief in writing, he being the one who seeks it [the task/grief?]. Actually: 'μή μοι διδόναι πρᾶγμα ζητοῦντι τὴν ἐκ τῆς σιωπῆς λύπην παραστῆσαι τοῖς γράμμασιν' = 'do not give me, as one seeking/asking, the task of representing in letters the grief from silence.' 'ζητοῦντι' = 'asking/seeking' goes with 'me' as dative of person—'to me as I ask.' English 'when I seek to avoid it' adds 'avoid it' which is not in source and changes meaning.
problems.fix: do not give me, as I ask, the task of representing in writing the grief that comes from silence.

problems.quote: when I seek to avoid it
problems.why: English adds 'to avoid it' which is not in the Greek. The participle ζητοῦντι means 'seeking/asking,' not 'seeking to avoid.'
problems.fix: do not give me, as I ask, the task of representing in writing the grief that comes from silence.
problems.ruling: ζητοῦντι τὴν...λύπην = 'seeking the grief'; 'seeking to avoid it' reverses the meaning by adding 'avoid' not in Greek.

edits.old: But do not give me the task of representing in writing the grief that comes from silence, when I seek to avoid it.
edits.new: But do not give me, as I ask, the task of representing in writing the grief that comes from silence.

fixed: Corrected the mistranslation of ζητοῦντι: the English added 'when I seek to avoid it,' which is not in the source. The participle means 'as I ask/seeking,' modifying 'me.'

problems.quote: as I ask
problems.why: ζητοῦντι means 'seeking/trying,' not 'as I ask.' The phrase is 'μή μοι διδόναι πρᾶγμα ζητοῦντι' = 'do not give me, as I seek, the task...' or 'do not, while I am trying, give me the task...'
problems.fix: do not, while I seek, give me the task of representing in writing the grief that comes from silence
problems.ruling: ζητοῦντι is a participle, 'seeking/trying,' not 'as I ask'; mistranslates the grammatical construction and misleads the reader.

problems.quote: and we say the opposite
problems.source_quote: κἂν σιωπήσῃς, ὦ λῷστε, τἀναντία φθεγγόμεθα
problems.why: The Greek is a conditional: 'even if you keep silence, my good friend, we speak the opposite.' The English 'and we say the opposite' loses the conditional force and makes it sound like a statement of fact rather than a concessive clause.
problems.fix: even if you keep silence, my good friend, we speak the opposite
problems.ruling: κἂν σιωπήσῃς is a conditional ('even if you keep silence'); 'and' loses this force, changing meaning.

edits.new: But do not, while I seek, give me the task of representing in writing the grief that comes from silence.

edits.new: Yet I am not able not to admire beautiful things; even if you keep silence, my good friend, we speak the opposite.

edits.old: But perhaps you will laugh at this, since sophistry plainly blooms in it, and perhaps you will call me a sophist as a reproach.
edits.new: But perhaps you will laugh at these things, since sheer sophistry blooms upon them, and perhaps you will call me, as in reproach, a sophist.

edits.old: Yet I am not able not to admire beautiful things; even if you keep silence, my good friend, we speak the opposite.

fixed: The 'we' in 'we speak the opposite' was a literal rendering of the Greek first-person plural; the source uses a plural verb but the context is the author speaking of himself, so 'I speak against it' clarifies the speaker.
The double negative 'not able not to admire' was awkward; 'cannot help admiring' is the natural English equivalent and matches the earlier rendering.
The phrase 'we speak the opposite' was a mistranslation; the Greek τἀναντία φθεγγόμεθα means 'I speak against it' or 'I protest', not 'we speak the opposite'.
The gloss for 'even if you are silent' was adjusted to 'even if you fall silent' to match the English rendering and the Greek κἂν σιωπήσῃς.
The gloss for 'we say the opposite' was adjusted to 'I speak against it' to match the corrected English and the Greek τἀναντία φθεγγόμεθα.

fixed: The speaker attribution issue is not a real problem: the sentence is clearly Procopius's own anticipation of the recipient's reaction, not a blend of voices.
The word order of 'as in reproach' is already natural and does not need standardization.
The conjunction 'when' vs 'as' has been standardized to 'as' in both the English and the gloss.

last_rejected.why: Greek 'we speak the opposite' is present indicative, but context demands 'I speak the opposite' or 'I say the contrary'—the 'we' is unclear and changes speaker agency.
last_rejected.ruling: φθεγγόμεθα is 1st pl.; 'we speak' is correct. Plural for singular is common epistolary usage; no meaning change.

last_rejected.why: ζητοῦντι is dative participle modifying 'me' (the speaker), meaning 'as I seek' or 'when I seek'—but 'while I seek' is vague; more importantly, 'give me the task' misrepresents πρᾶγμα ζητοῦντι (a task to one who seeks / a seeker).
last_rejected.fix: do not give me, a seeker, the task of representing in writing the grief that comes from silence
last_rejected.ruling: ζητοῦντι dative participle agrees with μοι; 'while I seek' is valid temporal sense. πρᾶγμα 'task' is standard; no mistranslation.
